newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish floods less grave than before - officials.
newsitem.headline: Polish floods less grave than before - officials.

text.p: The latest rain over Poland is making rivers overflow in parts of the southwest but overall damage will not be as bad as during floods caused by downpours two weeks ago, Poland's crisis committee said on Sunday.

Committee chief Zbigniew Sobotka told a news conference that levels in the Odra -- the major river flowing north along the German border which previously turned deadly and swamped towns and cities -- were generally lower than before.

"Smaller mountain rivers...are overflowing onto certain areas but the wave on the main rivers, on the Odra and the Wisla, is not a dangerous one which could bring devastation like the previous floods," Sobotka said.

Krzysztof Szamalek, a deputy environment minister on the crisis committee, said the rains were expected to lighten during the rest of Sunday and ease off on Monday, while forecasts for the rest of the week were optimistic.
Sobotka said the greatest risks now faced the Jelenia Gora, Legnica and Walbrzych provinces in the southwest, where rain overnight was significant. A few areas were under water.
Citizens and troops battled to construct sandbag barriers and strengthen dykes which were often broken or damaged by constant soaking.
The committee said no repeat of the previous grave floods in the major cities of Opole and Wroclaw on the Odra was expected.
As rains fell and new information arrived, the committee's list of flood devastation grew longer, setting out a balance sheet of human suffering.
The death toll rose by one to 50, while 5,400 sq km of land had been flooded of which about half was still swamped.
The floods had touched 1,107 towns and villages of which 254 were still flooded, 17 of them totally.
The committee said 140,000 people had been forced to evacuate their homes and 62,052 had not yet returned.
There were 40,800 troops and 22,300 fire officers involved in fighting the floods and in rescue efforts.
Government ministers have said the total damage will be in billions of zlotys but that it was still premature to start counting the costs in money terms. -- Steven Silber +48 22 653 9700
